title: Supreme Court Set for High-Stakes Showdown Over AR-15 Bans
snippet: The High Court will hear oral arguments on state and local restrictions targeting semi-automatic rifles, setting up one of the most consequential Second Amendment battles in modern history.
content:
WASHINGTON — Over a decade after the devastating mass shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School, the Supreme Court is stepping into the center of the nation's bitterest political fight: whether state and local governments have the constitutional authority to ban AR-15s and similar semi-automatic rifles.

The justices are scheduled to hear oral arguments Wednesday in a blockbuster Second Amendment challenge to laws enacted in Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois. The hearing marks the most significant gun control case to reach the court's 6-3 conservative supermajority in recent years, coming after a decade of escalating gun violence and a surge in public ownership of the controversial firearm.

A Divide Driven by Safety and Popularity

For municipal officials and gun control advocates, the effort to restrict weapons like the AR-15 is grounded in public safety. Proponents point to the unique lethality of semi-automatic long guns, arguing that their military-derived design, high muzzle velocity, and rapid-fire capability make them uniquely hazardous in civilian spaces.

"The basic function of government is to keep its citizenry safe," said Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke, who is arguing in defense of her jurisdiction's ban, highlighting the horrific toll such weapons take in mass casualty events.

Conversely, gun rights advocates and plaintiffs challenging the restrictions lean heavily on the sheer prevalence of the rifle. Industry estimates suggest that between 16 million and 26 million Americans currently own an AR-15 or similar platform, making it the single most popular rifle in the United States. Advocates contend that because the firearm is owned by millions of law-abiding citizens for lawful purposes, it is protected under the Constitution.

The Legal Standard: 'Common Use' vs. Historical Tradition

The legal clash will hinge largely on how the justices interpret two pivotal precedents: the 2008 District of Columbia v. Heller decision and the 2022 New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen ruling.

Under Heller, authored by the late Justice Antonin Scalia, the court established that arms in "common use" for self-defense are protected by the Second Amendment—a phrase repeated dozens of times in the plaintiffs' legal briefs. Gun rights groups argue that the vast number of AR-15s in circulation automatically places them in this protected category.

However, state and local officials defending the bans rely on Bruen, which requires modern firearm regulations to align with the nation's historical tradition of gun safety laws. Defenders of the bans have documented centuries of legal history—stretching back to English common law—restricting unusually dangerous or weaponized arms designed for battlefield combat.

All Eyes on the Bench

With conservative Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, and Brett Kavanaugh having previously expressed skepticism toward semi-automatic bans, the outcome of the case will likely rest on the votes of Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Amy Coney Barrett.

Legal analysts suggest both Roberts and Barrett could take a nuanced approach to the historical record, weighing the real-world safety implications of high-powered rifles against the broad constitutional protections established in recent rulings. The High Court's decision, expected by early summer, could either dismantle assault weapon restrictions nationwide or give state legislatures clear authority to regulate high-capacity firearms.
